title: Laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)
subtitle: Femtosecond or microkeratome flap, excimer stromal ablation and flap reposition

indications: Stable refractive error within the laser's range, in an adult with adequate corneal thickness and normal topography, who wants less dependence on glasses.
contraindications: Keratoconus or suspicious tomography, thin cornea or insufficient residual stromal bed, unstable refraction.
Severe dry eye, active ocular surface disease, uncontrolled autoimmune disease, pregnancy.
High risk of eye trauma (prefer surface ablation).
preparation: As for PRK, with calculated flap thickness and residual stromal bed (commonly at least 250 to 300 microns) and percent tissue altered.
Consent: flap complications, epithelial ingrowth, diffuse lamellar keratitis, ectasia, dry eye, glare and halos, enhancement, and presbyopia later.
positioning: Supine under the femtosecond laser and the excimer laser in turn, head level; fellow eye covered.
equipment: Femtosecond laser with suction interface (or microkeratome and suction ring), excimer laser with tracker, flap spatula, irrigating cannula, sponges, marking pen.
anatomy: The cornea: epithelium, Bowman's layer and anterior stroma lifted as a hinged flap of about 100 to 120 microns; the stromal bed beneath which is ablated.
criticalSafety: Correct eye and programme confirmed at both lasers.
If suction is lost during flap creation, do not lift a partial flap and do not ablate.
Reposition the flap carefully with no debris or striae.
commonErrors: Ablating on a buttonholed or incomplete flap.
Flap striae or a displaced flap.
complications: Flap complications (buttonhole, free cap, incomplete flap), flap striae or dislocation.
Diffuse lamellar keratitis, infection, epithelial ingrowth.
Dry eye, glare and halos, under- or over-correction.
postop: Shield at night for about a week; no rubbing; antibiotic and steroid drops.
Review the next day to check the flap.
Same-day return for pain or falling vision.

steps.emphasis: Elective surgery on healthy eyes: written consent at a separate visit.
At each laser: patient, eye, refraction and treatment read aloud.
Supine under each laser in turn, head level; fellow eye covered.
Topical anaesthetic drops; an oral anxiolytic per local practice.
Clean the lids, drape the lashes away.
Shield at night, no rubbing, review the next day.

step.lasik.flap.title: Creating the corneal flap
step.lasik.flap.why: The flap gives LASIK its fast, painless recovery but is also where its specific complications come from. Suction and a stable interface decide whether the flap is complete and even.
how: Mark the cornea so the flap can be realigned.
Dock the suction interface centred on the cornea; check suction before creating the flap.
Create the flap with the femtosecond laser (or microkeratome) with the planned diameter, depth and superior or nasal hinge.

step.lasik.suction-loss.title: Bailout: suction loss or an incomplete flap
step.lasik.suction-loss.why: A flap cut through after suction loss can be irregular, thin or incomplete. Lifting it and ablating risks irregular astigmatism; stopping and treating later is safe.
how: If suction breaks during flap creation, stop. With a femtosecond laser, redocking and repeating may be possible per the manufacturer.

If the flap is incomplete, buttonholed or a free cap, do not lift it and do not ablate: replace it, protect it, and plan surface ablation or a new flap after the cornea has settled (often three months).
Record what happened and tell the patient.
pitfalls: Lifting and ablating on a buttonholed flap.

step.lasik.flap-lift.title: Lifting the flap
step.lasik.flap-lift.why: A clean lift exposes the bed evenly for the ablation without tearing the flap or the hinge.
how: Under the excimer microscope, open the flap edge with a spatula and lift it smoothly to the hinge.
Fold it back onto a dry surface, protecting the hinge from the laser.
pitfalls: Letting the flap lie where it will be ablated.

step.lasik.reposition.title: Flap reposition and interface irrigation
step.lasik.reposition.why: Debris or folds left in the interface cause inflammation, striae and poor vision. Careful reposition is the end of the operation, not an afterthought.
how: Lay the flap back and irrigate the interface to wash out debris.
Smooth the flap from the hinge outwards with a moist sponge; align the marks and the gutter evenly all round.
Wait for adherence, then check for striae at the slit lamp or microscope before the patient leaves.
